doc.title: Wilson "Chembo" Corniel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

chapter: Learning the drums and early career
title: Learning percussion without resources, Boys Harbor and Bobby Rodriguez Y La Compania
summary: Compared with today's written material, he learned from records, neighborhood percussionists, watching conga players and Boys Harbor School of Music, then joined Bobby Rodriguez Y La Compania in 1977.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Jazz for decades was mostly learned by finding a mentor and listening, aurally, and now it’s a big business in education, and thousands of books and manuals on how to improvise and all that. Has the same thing happened with Latin music as far as now you can, all this stuff you’re talking about is now written down?

Oh yes. Oh yes definitely. You know because when I was a kid trying to find information we didn’t have YouTube, we didn’t have the internet. I had my album, I’d put on a record and I would hear the conga player but you would hear the dominant hand and you didn’t know what the left hand was doing so therefore you were doing it wrong because you had

to see that there’s a certain technique that fills in the whole pattern of a tumbao. All you hear is [scats] see that’s the right hand only. But what’s this one doing? There’s another, there’s the other half that you’re learning. So you start picking up bad habits already until somebody who knows, and I got in contact with these people that moved in my neighborhood, professional percussionists that were playing with Eddie Palmieri in the 70s, and they seen that I had a little bit of talent so they took me up and cleaned me up and polished — then I was on my way even further. Then I learned how to read music on top of that. And then after that — which conga players, they never gave a chart to. They only give it to the brass players. I had to come with a cassette player and record the rehearsal and then memorize eight songs, all the breaks and all that stuff. This is how we did it. We didn’t have the internet and they didn’t teach you how to read. We didn’t have Latin music in the schools. We didn’t even have a conga in the school, we just had maracas and a guiro, which they called a fish. You know, the colored ones? You know? That was that guiro. You have the guiro for the cha cha cha. You know? We got a fish and some maracas. That was the extent of Latin music in my school. The rest I learned in the street. You know. We all had a conga, we go to the park and start playing, and then from there I got my sound, we got rhythms but we didn’t know what we were doing but we were just banging and got a little groove always happening, the same groove but we kept for hours and hours and hours and days and days and days so I bumped into a lot of people here. I started — I was old enough to go to the clubs and seeing the professional bands and I would just stay there the whole night just in the corner looking at the conga player and seeing his hands and what he’s doing, then I would practice it the next day you know, I would try to memorize some riffs you know. Then they started to open up a school, Boys Harbor School of Music in Harlem and then I went there where they’re all Latinos, they had a piano, bass, vocals, percussion, and then that’s where we started learning, those guys were helping us kids to read now and play the right rhythms and how to lock in and the concept of playing with the clave and playing together. So after a couple of years of that then I landed a gig with one of the top bands, when I was young, in 1977 Bobby Rodriguez Y La Compania we were like a band of kids, we were only 21 anyway. And we had a sound of Latin mix, because the leader was a sax player and he played clarinet. So we had a Dixieland salsa kind of a sound. So we would do some Dixieland stuff, because he had a clarinet, no other horns. Salsa band had the clarinet. So the brass was a trumpet, tenor, trombone. So you’ve got a lot of colors with those three. So the tenor player was the leader and he played flute, soprano and clarinet. So we go into a bebop swing [scats] and he would blow, like New Orleans style, you know. So we would mix that with Latin, it was something new and fresh and the people were dancing to it. You know so that band really put me on the map and started my career you know.
